articles.title: State officials offered to store nuclear waste. Then residents found out.
articles.summary: HARPERS FERRY, W.Va. - The jagged limestone rocks of Old Standard Quarry have weathered many eras of history. The property was the site of a Civil War battle...
articles.body:
State officials offered to store nuclear waste. Then residents found out.

HARPERS FERRY, W.Va. - The jagged limestone rocks of Old Standard Quarry have weathered many eras of history. The property was the site of a Civil War battle, then a quarry and is now a popular destination for bungee jumping, its dark green water fed by a natural spring.

Recently, the state proposed yet another use for the land: as storage for radioactive nuclear waste from around the country.

"I thought it was a joke," said Pasha Majdi, president of the Jefferson County Commission. "It doesn't make any sense."

It wasn't a joke. Without consulting residents or local officials, Gov. Patrick Morrisey's energy office submitted a detailed pitch to the Trump administration offering the Jefferson County quarry and three other sites for a potential "Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus."

The Trump administration has said such campuses would need to agree to store spent nuclear fuel - one of the nation's most vexing environmental problems - in exchange for federal support for research, development and production facilities that aim to modernize and grow the country's nuclear power infrastructure.

The administration claims the campuses could create 25,000 jobs and generate tens of billions of dollars in private investment and tax revenue. Those economics are alluring to states eager for development.

Twenty-six expressed some manner of interest before the federal government chose Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Idaho and West Virginia as finalists.

"West Virginia is intentionally beginning with nuclear initiatives that are actionable and high‑value, particularly those tied to the spent and partially spent fuel stream and backend services, areas where the state can quickly demonstrate success and build momentum," the state's pitch promised. It assured that "West Virginia recognizes that for any project with potential community impacts, social buy-in and community alignment are foundational."

But the way things played out in West Virginia underscored how community anxiety around nuclear waste is not easily overcome. That anxiety is why there is no comprehensive plan for permanently disposing of the tens of thousands of tons of spent fuel that already exists in the United States, much less for getting rid of the waste that could be generated with the quadrupling of nuclear power capacity President Donald Trump envisions.

As soon as details of the West Virginia proposal were disclosed, thanks to a public records request by the Charleston Gazette-Mail, the backlash was intense. Days after dismissing the report as "fake news," Morrisey (R) withdrew the state from consideration altogether.

The Morrisey administration did not respond to requests for comment.

Energy Department spokesman Ben Dietderich said in an emailed statement that "the program has proven to be a huge success - with more than 25 states applying to participate - much of that success can be attributed [to] allowing states and local communities decide for themselves if an innovation campus is right for them."

The West Virginia episode, though, left communities bewildered, the governor politically wounded and the nuclear waste problem unresolved.

The nuclear life cycle campus competition comes after the federal government tried - and failed - to create a repository for spent fuel for decades. Congress had designated Yucca Mountain, Nevada, as the most suitable place for it. But local opposition derailed that plan.

Now, the focus is on finding a "consent-based" solution that would be developed in coordination with communities interested in developing facilities. Such a model has been successful in parts of Europe. It typically takes many years of deliberation and negotiation by the communities involved.

"I'm personally a bit skeptical that states are going to move as fast as the [Trump] administration wants or is expecting," said Matt Bowen, a nuclear scholar at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy who has been tracking the life cycle campus initiative.

The difficult conversations state officials need to have with the cities and counties that would host nuclear campuses are just getting underway. Nuclear industry officials say states taking a deliberative, democratic approach are getting genuine interest from communities that are viable candidates for a campus.

In West Virginia, though, state officials appear not to have communicated with each other or the towns they were offering up in their pitch. And their experience shows how quickly the process can go sideways.

Far from the fast-growing Harpers Ferry region, in economically struggling Boone County, the state's nuclear pitch called for storing waste at what was once one of the largest mountaintop-removal coal mines in the country - an environmentally damaged site the state and local community have for years been seeking to convert into a redevelopment opportunity. The former coal-mining stronghold has lost nearly one-fifth of its population since 2010, as jobs disappeared.

But the nuclear campus proposal landed with a thud there, too. Local opposition quickly emerged. The area's state representative expressed frustration on social media that the community had not been consulted and relief when the state scrapped the proposal.

The proposal had highlighted the potential benefits of a new state law, written for data center developers, that allows for fast-track approval of permits while bypassing local governments.

"It felt for many of us like: 'Here we go again,'" said Christine Wimer, president of the Jefferson County Foundation, a conservation advocacy group. "This is the same old thing in West Virginia. People come here. They get the good stuff. We get taken advantage of.'"

Wimer said everything about the site the state was proposing near Harpers Ferry was unworkable. The porous limestone is particularly ill-suited for storing toxic materials. Half the property is a federally protected conservation zone, forever honoring its status as a historic battlefield. The other half, she said, is underwater.

"Limestone essentially works like a highway for waste," said Cara Keys, a county commissioner, as she stood over the quarry. "You could put something here, and it could infect someone's well 20 miles away. The fact that they thought this could be a nuclear waste dump is very concerning."

Steve Pearson, editor of Jefferson County's Observer Weekly newspaper, dove deep into the details of the proposal and emerged perplexed how it ever got submitted. "Even if you just wanted to build a warehouse, you could not do it there," he said. "There is no land for it."

Down the road from the quarry in Middleway, a remarkably well-preserved village of 18th- and 19th-century stone, brick and log buildings on the National Register of Historic Places, farmers were already exhausted trying to stop plans for a large water-bottling plant that developers are seeking to build over the vociferous objections of community leaders, who warn it would be an environmental mess. The news that the state hoped to store nuclear waste nearby left them stunned.

"I like to be left alone," said David Liskey, 75, who has been in the area all his life. His ancestors started farming there in the mid-1700s. "People like it here the way it is. We don't want what they are talking about doing."

Gabby Wilson has only been in the area a short time, having recently relocated from North Carolina. But Wilson, the owner of Prismatic Art Studio in downtown Charles Town, was every bit as blunt as Liskey.

"It's just gross," she said of the nuclear campus proposal. "We moved here to get away from things like that."

articles.title: 400-plus Indian-origin scholars, alumni from 27 countries warn against ‘anarchy’
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Days after competing groups of Harvard-linked Indians took opposing positions on protests against the Election Commission, more than 400
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Days after competing groups of Harvard-linked Indians took opposing positions on protests against the Election Commission, more than 400 Indian-origin students, researchers and alumni associated with universities across 27 countries have issued a statement warning against efforts to erode public trust in constitutional institutions and attempts to replace democratic debate with street confrontation.Titled “Spare India from Anarchy”, the statement carries 402 names, including individuals linked to Harvard, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Oxford, Cambridge, Stanford, Princeton, Yale and Columbia universities, as well as the London School of Economics, National University of Singapore and University of Toronto.The signatories allege that “a frenzy of election denial” and a preference for ‘street over Sansad’ have taken hold in some quarters. They argue that unfavourable election results are being used to question electoral procedures, adverse court rulings to cast doubts on judicial independence and even the armed forces are being drawn into partisan debate.“An unconscionable and devious plan of sowing seeds of doubt in Indian democracy has been hatched,” the statement claims, accusing unspecified groups of turning matters before courts into campaigns on the streets.The intervention follows a public disagreement among Harvard affiliates over the October 10 protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. A group of around 100 Harvard-linked signatories criticised alleged police excesses and detentions, while 44 others subsequently warned against attacks on the credibility of constitutional institutions.The latest appeal widens that dispute beyond Harvard, though it does not name the Election Commission, the SIR exercise or the Delhi protests explicitly.Invoking BR Ambedkar’s warning about the “grammar of anarchy”, the statement says dissent remains essential to democracy but should not become a cover for undermining its institutions. It calls for resolving differences through “debate, discussion, dialogue and dissent” within the constitutional framework.The accompanying document says the signatories are based in, or have studied in, countries across four continents. It also makes clear that the listed university affiliations do not amount to endorsements by the institutions themselves.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2011, a British couple bought a crumbling 10-storey Victorian water tower for £380,000 and spent about £2 million converting it into a home; after a £2.5 million sale, it is now listed for £2.75 million
articles.summary: A Grade II-listed Victorian water tower that featured in a memorable episode of Channel 4's Grand Designs is back on the market for £2.75 million after
articles.body: A Grade II-listed Victorian water tower that featured in a memorable episode of Channel 4's Grand Designs is back on the market for £2.75 million after previously selling for £2.5 million. Located in Kennington, south London, the 10-storey landmark was bought in 2011 for £380,000 by partners Leigh Osborne and Graham Voce. Over the next two years, they spent around £2 million on major repairs and modern additions to turn the abandoned structure into a luxury five-bedroom home. The transformation featured in the 100th episode of Grand Designs in 2012, hosted by Kevin McCloud. After putting the finished property up for sale for as much as £6.5 million in 2018, the owners gradually lowered the asking price. They eventually sold the unusual home in 2021 for around £2.5 million. The property has now returned to the market, with estate agents listing it for £2.75 million.Overcoming budget spikes and construction hurdlesWhen Osborne and Voce bought the 1867 water tower, it was in very poor condition. The building was filled with pigeon droppings, crumbling brickwork and rotting timber. The couple first expected to spend around £600,000 on the restoration. However, structural problems and changes to their ambitious design pushed the cost up to nearly £2 million. To cover the rising expenses, the owners stretched their finances to the limit. They used several personal loans and credit cards to pay for the work. The renovation included adding a multi-storey glass extension, nicknamed "The Cube", at the base of the tower. It created a large, modern living space beneath the original brick structure. At the top, the tower's historic cast-iron water tank was turned into a main bedroom suite with 360-degree views across London's skyline.Architectural features and historic linksThe 100-foot-tall tower has a long history. It was built in 1867 to supply water to the Lambeth Workhouse. The surrounding grounds were also linked to the childhood of famous comedy actor Charlie Chaplin, who lived at the workhouse with his mother during the late 19th century. The updated property covers more than 4,000 square feet across several floors, connected by an internal lift and a central staircase. Key features of the conversion include:A living and dining room with glass walls inside the modern ground-floor extension.Five bedrooms and four bathrooms spread across the main tower.A top-floor viewing room and an outdoor rooftop terrace with clear views of landmarks such as Big Ben and the Shard.Original exposed brickwork combined with energy-efficient, triple-glazed windows.Market trajectory and estate listingsAfter the project was completed in 2012, the property first went on sale in 2018 with an asking price of £6.5 million. However, it failed to attract a buyer at that price. The owners reduced the asking price several times over the next three years. In mid-2021, buyer Jamie Hamer purchased the property for around £2.5 million. At the time, Hamer said the top-floor viewing area and views of central London made the home feel like owning a private castle. Recent listings from estate agencies including The Modern House and Foxtons show that the Kennington water tower is back on the market with a guide price of £2,750,000. The agencies' listings highlight its rare status as a Zone 1 architectural landmark that combines Victorian engineering with modern luxury interiors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Opposition targets Pune mayor over ‘not a contractor’ remark
articles.summary: Opposition slams Pune mayor Manjusha Nagpure’s “not a contractor” remark after Yerawada tragedy; protests planned, BJP urges stricter safety norms.
articles.body: Pune: The Yerawada tragedy has snowballed into a political controversy, with opposition parties attacking Pune mayor Manjusha Nagpure over her ‘insensitive’ remarks in the aftermath. Responding to a query, Nagpure allegedly said she was “not a contractor” and had not “pushed the man”.NCP (SP) MLA Rohit Pawar accused the mayor of displaying insensitivity. “Such a response is unbecoming of the city’s first citizen. At a time when a family is grieving, this reflects a shocking lack of empathy,” Pawar said.Shiv Sena’s Pune unit announced plans to launch protests over inadequate safety measures at public work sites, alleging that the BJP-backed civic administration had failed to enforce basic safeguards. Shiv Sena city chief Pramod Bhangire said, “Responsibility for the tragedy should extend beyond contractors to civic officials overseeing the project. There are deep-rooted irregularities in the drainage department and other public works. The decline in quality and safety is a direct result of these practices.”Responding to the criticism, BJP city chief Dheeraj Ghate said the party had taken up the matter with civic authorities and urged stricter enforcement of safety norms to prevent similar incidents.The tragedy has intensified demands for accountability, with citizens insisting that administrative notices alone are not enough and that criminal liability must be fixed for preventable deaths caused by negligence in public infrastructure projects.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Defunct Moradabad IMFL unit restarts operations
articles.summary: Defunct Moradabad IMFL bottling unit restarts; Allied Blenders takes over Rs 70 crore plant, adds 60 lakh cases/year capacity and plans ENA expansion.
articles.body: Lucknow: A defunct liquor bottling unit in Moradabad restarted commercial operations on Monday after being revived, marking a fresh capacity addition in Uttar Pradesh’s IMFL manufacturing base. The facility, with an initial production capacity of 60 lakh cases of Indian-made foreign liquor annually, will be operated by Allied Blenders and Distillers Limited.The company took over the plant in Jan 2026 for Rs 70 crore. The unit was earlier run by National Industrial Corporation Limited before operations shut down.Allied Blenders said the Moradabad facility will, over time, also be leveraged to expand its extra neutral alcohol production, a move aimed at reducing reliance on external channel partners and improving supply chain control.Managing director Amar Sinha said the start of operations would strengthen the company’s footprint in Uttar Pradesh and support its strategy of backward integration. articles.title: Harsimrat writes to Shah, seeks CBI probe into Jhota murder
articles.summary: Harsimrat Kaur Badal writes to Amit Shah seeking CBI probe into anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota’s murder and alleged politician-police-drug mafia nexus in Punjab.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Shiromani Akali Dal MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal has written to Union home minister Amit Shah seeking a CBI probe into the murder of anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota in Mansa and a wider investigation into the alleged politician-police-drug mafia nexus in Punjab.In a letter dated Oct 18, the Bathinda MP alleged that Jhota was killed after exposing “the illegal sale of controlled pharmaceutical substances and synthetic drugs in the region”.She sought an investigation into the role of police officials, drug inspectors and political leaders in the drug trade and the killing.Enclosing a statement, which she claimed was submitted by Jhota’s father, Bhim Singh, to the police, Harsimrat said the family had raised questions about the alleged shielding of drug offenders and threats against the activist.She claimed Bhim Singh named several police officials, accusing them of involvement in the drug trade and responsibility for his son’s death.Harsimrat also questioned the response to Jhota’s call to a local police officer before he went to a medical store where he was subsequently shot.She flagged the firearm licence held by the accused, Ashwani Kumar.Kumar was “accused of selling controlled psychotropic drugs several times and had also been jailed for some time but was able to procure a weapon licence which the then Mansa SSP approved in 2024, a few months after he was released from jail”.The MP urged Shah to include other cases involving people who spoke against drugs, including those of Mohanjit Singh of Sunam and Gulzar Singh, in a comprehensive investigation into alleged action against anti-drug activists.Jhota was shot dead in Mansa on October 13. Ashwani Kumar was arrested in connection with the case.“There are numerous other cases of whistleblowers being forced into silence even as drug traffickers have a field day in Punjab. articles.title: 'Why have you traveled to China': Indian family with an infant denied US visa for a vacation
articles.summary: Amid several accounts of B1/B2 visa denials for Indian travelers this year, one account stood out as the woman pointed out a particular question that she
articles.body: Amid several accounts of B1/B2 visa denials for Indian travelers this year, one account stood out as the woman pointed out a particular question that she and her husband were asked during their visa interview. The woman narrated her interview experience on Reddit and clarified that her husband and she applied for a tourist visa as they were planning for a US vacation trip with their infant.The husband and the wife were asked the general question about whether they had any fear to return to India, a question that every visa applicant gets asked to ensure that they won't be claiming asylum once they enter the US. When asked, they told the visa officer that their budget for the US trip was Rs 15 lakh and they were planning the trip with a travel agent. They informed the visa officer about their job, positions and experience. They also disclosed their travel history to Australia, Thailand, Maldives and Bali."Why have you traveled to China?" the visa officer asked the husband. The man replied that it was a work visit and his office is headquartered in China.This was more or less the end of the interview. The visa officer asked two more questions: whether they have only one child and whether they have anyone living in the US. They said they had only one child and no one in the US and they were planning to stay in hotels.Their visa was denied. The Redditor sought help in understanding why their visas were denied.Redditors point out vague answers, clear immigrant intentRedditors pointed out that while it is more common to get a US B1/B2 visa denied on the first attempt, there were probably many red flags in this particular case. They said it is unlikely for an Indian family with an infant to plan a US trip unless they know someone there. The answers should have more specific itineraries like the names of the hotels they were planning to stay at and the places they were planning to visit, one said. Also, the involvement of a travel agent seemed a red flag to many. "You should mention where you want to stay (specific name of the hotel), for how long (specific date), the details of your itinerary (example: you want to go to NYC to see the Empire State Building, Brooklyn Bridge etc). otherwise, the officer would think you're a potential illegal immigrant," one suggested."While it’s already difficult to get a visa, working for a “Chinese” company doesn’t help too in these times," another wrote.You use AI every day.
